n: Ezekiel opens with a date and a place: he is among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, beside the Chebar canal, when the heavens open to him. The “thirtieth year” is probably his own age—the age when priests began serving.

f.g: Likely Ezekiel’s age; priests began full service at thirty.
A large irrigation canal near the city of Nippur in Babylonia.

n: The fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s exile dates the vision to about 593 BC. Jehoiachin and many leaders—Ezekiel included—had been deported in 597 BC, about a decade before Jerusalem’s final fall.

f.g: Also called Jeconiah or Coniah; king of Judah for three months before surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar.

n: Ezekiel is a priest, son of Buzi. Though far from the temple, he receives God’s word in a pagan land—a powerful message that the Lord is not confined to Jerusalem. “The hand of the LORD” signals prophetic power resting on him.

f.g: Another name for the Babylonians, from the ruling dynasty’s homeland in southern Mesopotamia.

f.w: the hand of the LORD was there upon him

n: Ezekiel sees a storm sweeping in from the north: a huge cloud, flashing fire, and a glowing radiance at its center. Storm, cloud, and fire are classic signs of God’s presence, as at Sinai.

f.g: A stormy wind.

f.w: a great cloud, and a fire

f.g: Hebrew ḥashmal—a gleaming substance, perhaps electrum (a gold-silver alloy). Its exact meaning is uncertain.

n: Out of the fire appear four living creatures with an overall human shape. Chapter 10 identifies them as cherubim, heavenly beings who attend God’s throne.
Each creature has four faces and four wings—able to face every direction at once, fitting servants of a God who sees everything.

f.g: Isaiah’s seraphim had six wings.

n: Their legs are straight, their feet like a calf’s hoof, and they gleam like polished bronze—images of strength, steadiness, and brilliance.

f.g: Polished bronze.

n: Under their wings they have human hands. Later one creature uses its hands to pass burning coals (10:7–8).
Their wings touch one another, and they move straight ahead without turning, since with faces on every side they never need to turn around.

f.w: they turned not when they went
f.g: They could move in any direction without turning.

n: The four faces—human, lion, ox, and eagle—are often understood as representing the best of creation: humanity, wild animals, domestic animals, and birds. Early Christians linked them with the four Gospel writers.

f.w: the face of a man, and the face of a lion

n: Two of each creature’s wings stretch upward to touch its neighbors, and two cover its body—an act of reverence before God.
The creatures move wherever “the spirit” directs them, in perfect obedience and unity.

f.w: whither the spirit was to go, they went
f.g: The Hebrew ruaḥ can mean spirit, wind, or will.

n: The creatures glow like burning coals and torches, with fire darting among them and lightning flashing out—an overwhelming display of holy power.
They dart back and forth like flashes of lightning—swift and dazzling.

f.w: as the appearance of a flash of lightning

n: Next Ezekiel notices a wheel on the ground beside each creature. The vision is becoming a chariot-throne—God on the move.

f.g: Later Jewish mystics called this vision the merkavah, the “chariot.”

n: The wheels sparkle like a precious stone, and each seems to be a wheel within a wheel—perhaps two wheels set crosswise so they can roll in any direction.

f.g: Hebrew tarshish, a gleaming gemstone, perhaps topaz or chrysolite.

f.w: a wheel in the middle of a wheel
f.g: Likely intersecting wheels, allowing movement in all four directions.

n: The wheels can go in any of the four directions without turning, matching the creatures.

f.w: they turned not when they went
f.g: The phrase echoes v. 9 and v. 12, stressing perfect, direct obedience.

n: The wheels’ rims are towering and awe-inspiring, and covered with eyes—a picture of God’s all-seeing knowledge.

f.g: The rims of the wheels.

n: Wheels and creatures move together, whether rolling on the ground or rising into the air.
The spirit that moves the creatures also moves the wheels. The whole chariot acts as one under God’s direction.

f.w: the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels
f.g: The wheels share the creatures’ life and will.

n: A repetition for emphasis: when the creatures go, stand, or rise, the wheels do the same. God’s presence is mobile—able to come even to exiles in Babylon.
Above the creatures’ heads stretches a platform like dazzling crystal—a sky-like dome.

f.g: An expanse or platform, the same word used for the sky in Genesis.
Awe-inspiring ice or crystal.

n: Beneath the platform each creature spreads two wings toward its neighbors and covers its body with the other two.

f.g: A posture of reverence and modesty before God.

n: The sound of their wings is like roaring waters, like the voice of the Almighty, like the noise of an army camp—sound as overwhelming as the sight.

f.w: like the noise of great waters

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai, an ancient name of God.

n: When the creatures stop and lower their wings, a voice comes from above the platform.

f.g: The source of authority is above the creatures—God himself.

n: Above the platform is a throne of sapphire-blue stone, and on it a figure who looks like a man. Ezekiel speaks carefully—“the likeness,” “the appearance”—because he is describing God. Latter-day Saints see here a witness that God has a glorified form in whose image man was made.

f.g: Probably lapis lazuli, deep blue.

f.w: the likeness as the appearance of a man

n: The figure glows like gleaming metal surrounded by fire, from the waist up and the waist down—radiant glory too bright to describe exactly.

f.g: Waist, hips.

n: The brightness is like a rainbow in the clouds—a symbol of God’s covenant faithfulness. Ezekiel concludes: this was the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Overwhelmed, he falls on his face and hears a voice speaking.

f.w: the bow that is in the cloud
